pull.title: net: reimplement private broadcast as jobs isolated from the node
pull.body:
Split out of #36608, the overall private broadcast rework to support ease of review for like-for-like feature.

Differences from #36608 :
1. No tool support or prep refactors for the tool
2. No package relay
3. Slimmed down test profile focusing on protecting aginst IP address linkage and not crashing the node on adversarial inputs (which is a leak in itself)

With `-privatebroadcast`, `sendrawtransaction` queues a job instead of handing the transaction to
the connection manager. Each job runs on its own thread, shares no state with the node, and
reaches the network only through the Tor proxy: it resolves the chain's DNS seeds, then announces
over BIP324 to recipients on a schedule drawn up front, each connection with fresh isolation
credentials. Nothing a recipient does, and nothing the node sees of the transaction coming back,
changes the plan, and the transaction enters the node's mempool only when it returns from the
network. The old private broadcast connections and relay are removed.

The invariants are specified in `doc/design/private-broadcast.md`.

The rest of the tests are in a follow-up to be considered later:
https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/tree/2026-10-pb_reimpl_followup

This PR's tests do not check that each attempt gets its own VERSION nonce, PING nonce and BIP324 key (A4 in `doc/design/private-broadcast.md`), so a regression there would pass.

On 19f9cd7c4d I made each of these values a constant for the whole process, one line in `src/privbcast/attempt.cpp` at a time. All four `p2p_private_broadcast*.py` tests passed on each of the three variants. Constant proxy credentials, by contrast, make `p2p_private_broadcast.py` fail.

Your [follow-up branch](https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/tree/2026-10-pb_reimpl_followup) already checks all three, in `p2p_private_broadcast_job.py`; I ran it on the PING-nonce variant and it fails there. A reused nonce or key lets recipients link a node's broadcasts to each other, the same kind of leak as the IP linkage the kept tests guard against. Could that check move into this PR?

@fametrano willing to be convinced to move particular items to this PR, but I'm really focusing on IP address level leaks for the first PR. Preventing cross-attempt or cross-tx fingerprinting is a secondary goal, and hard to achieve arbitrary level of assurances, hence its deferral. 

edit: changed my mind and brought it forward

I find the following not acceptable:

Relying on DNS seeds
--------------------

Currently DNS seeds are used only to bootstrap a new node. That happens once in its lifetime and there is a fallback mechanism if the DNS seeds do not work. We never rely solely only on DNS seeds for something. They are centralized services.

`doc/dnsseed-policy.md` mentions:

> Bitcoin Core attempts to minimize the level of trust in DNS seeds

I do not think that it is reasonable to start relying on a few servers permanently (not just once in a lifetime, but every time a node wants to privately broadcast a transaction). This means that if a few operators decide to switch off (or misbehave) their services then everybody on the network is obstructed from privately broadcasting their transactions. That resembles more a client-server architecture than a decentralized P2P network.

Not broadcasting to Tor or I2P peers
------------------------------------

Only broadcasting to IP peers via the Tor network would make the feature too fragile - it would rely on the Tor network and the Tor exit nodes working properly. The Tor network has been down in the past. I think it is important to have a fallback mechanism which currently is the I2P network. Also, right now we do not rely on the Tor exit nodes. We could broadcast a transaction within the Tor network to an `.onion` peer even if the exit nodes are off or misbehaving.

Even moderate adoption of private broadcast in its current form improves the privacy of everybody because everybody could be a recipient. Privacy is improved even for nodes that broadcast-to-all. That would be spoiled if we only send to IP peers. Note that a private broadcast recipient would further broadcast-to-all the newly received transaction in a way that is indistinguishable from them being the transaction originator. So an observer can no longer tell whether a node is the original sender or was a recipient of a private broadcast. For this to work everybody must be a potential private broadcast recipient.

> I do not think that it is reasonable to start relying on a few servers permanently (not just once in a lifetime, but every time a node wants to privately broadcast a transaction). This means that if a few operators decide to switch off (or misbehave) their services then everybody on the network is obstructed from privately broadcasting their transactions. That resembles more a client-server architecture than a decentralized P2P network.

If the seeds go offline, private broadcast stops; it doesn't leak. If they misbehave, the most they can do is pick recipients that drop the transaction. They can't learn who is sending. 

The alternative of picking Tor/i2p peers from addrman as master does, is not an answer anyone should be happy with.

Today we give attackers significant influence over choices being made by victim. Peers can be influenced, by design, into dialing to peers that are unique fingerprints, with the attacker writing to their addrman.

Tor isn't decentralized either, but we accept utility in terms of privacy.

> I think it is important to have a fallback mechanism which currently is the I2P network. 

Currently in master, it makes sybiling victims much easier, which results in an IP address leak, which is an unfortunate side-effect of the current architecture. Assuming we adopted something like this PR, then we would have to introduce a "just in time" gathering of addresses, which would *still* be going through seeder nodes, or again, reintroducing fundamental leaks via local addrman usage. No free lunch here.

> Even moderate adoption of private broadcast in its current form improves the privacy of everybody because everybody could be a recipient. Privacy is improved even for nodes that broadcast-to-all. 

The attacks it resists are quite limited today, and therefore it's sort of in purgatory where we can't make any promises about it. That's quite sad, and completely avoidable.

The design doc looks AI written; is it meant for human or agentic consumption? Shouldn't it be a BIP, or at least posted to the mailing list for broader discussion on exactly the sort of tradeoffs vasild raises [above](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36628#issuecomment-6413061893)?

+6k lines (+3.5k -1k under src excluding test) seems like a lot. Presumably also AI written with light human review?

If the idea is to separate this from the node, it seems like having a separate binary interacting lightly with the node might be a better structure. Something like: a "bitcoin-privbcast" binary, connects only over i2p/tor, keeps it own addrman independent from the node, initially populated from dns seeds, perhaps updated in some way (again, independent of the node), bitcoind wallet sends private broadcast txs via bitcoin-privbcast's stdin, and then just monitors for them to appear in the mempool (and sends a cancel message to privbcast's stdin when that occurs), and bitcoin-privbcast rate limits, retries, expires them itself to avoid send bursts correlating with the node restarting.

That approach would allow people with higher or different tx privacy goals to replace the privbcast binary with something custom if desired (eg to make different tradeoffs about addr handling, or using tor exit nodes, etc), without needing to modify bitcoind source.

> The design doc looks AI written; is it meant for human or agentic consumption?

The PR text is AI written, curated a number of times under my direction as the primary document. I think there's great value for both humans and AI. It doesn't have to be in the merged branch.

> Shouldn't it be a BIP, or at least posted to the mailing list for broader discussion on exactly the sort of tradeoffs vasild raises https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36628#issuecomment-6413061893?

I think there's definitely value increasing anonymity set if nothing else. By the same token, the current implementation should have gone through a BIP process, for exactly the same reasons.

> That approach 

Originally I designed it as a separate tool, but I was hoping for a like-for-like replacement. However the architecture lends itself just fine to it, as the only coupled code in this PR to the node is the queue portion. An "addrman but not node's addrman" is another design quest, because resisting cross-tx correlation, while a secondary goal, is worth trying to preserve under adversaries. 

> appear in the mempool (and sends a cancel message to privbcast's stdin when that occurs),

This is a leak. I prefer bounded tries. We could have it do retries based on block non-inclusion or some other criteria that isn't a clear fingerprint, e.g., not enough peers asking for the tx itself.

> Peers can be influenced, by design, into dialing to peers that are unique fingerprints, with the attacker writing to their addrman.

Can this design be expanded on about how they can be influenced, and why that is by design? Would this mean the problem is with the design that allows peers to be influenced into dialing to peers that are unique fingerprints, and not the actual private broadcast? Perhaps this can be solved by a better upstream design in addrman?

> Currently in master, it makes sybiling victims much easier, which results in an IP address leak

Would that be a problem with i2p in general, and not private broadcast? I'm not sure I understand how a sybil attack in i2p could leak a clearnet IP address.

How would sybiling the node affect sending private broadcast transactions through ephemeral i2p tunnels? These connections should not be connected in any way to the broadcasting node's long-lived i2p address (if it has one) or their tor onion address or clearnet addresses.

> The attacks it resists are quite limited today

Since we no longer make any promises, and this is marked experimental, can we elaborate on the attacks it cannot resist? I find it difficult to reason about the tradeoffs presented here with respect to attacks that I do not understand or know about. Similarly with the above claims about peer influence and i2p sybiling. Wasn't part of the benefit of marking experimental to allow these attacks and weaknesses to be discussed openly?

> Can this design be expanded on about how they can be influenced, and why that is by design? Would this mean the problem is with the design that allows peers to be influenced into dialing to peers that are unique fingerprints, and not the actual private broadcast? Perhaps this can be solved by a better upstream design in addrman?

Ok I was a bit sloppy in my wording: the design *permits* influencing, as an accepted residual.

Addrman is built for partition resistance with the goal of finding a single honest peer that will give us the heaviest chain. As long as the attackers can't take all slots, the node is protected.

In the private broadcast scenario, our goals are different: the choice of recipient must not say anything about who made it. Each node's table is different, and anyone can write to it through addr gossip, directly as a peer or relayed through one. Addrman needs one honest peer to stay safe; private broadcast loses privacy to one dishonest peer that can "read" these differences.

A "fixed" addrman would be one that doesn't allow peers to write to it, which would remove its whole purpose. A separate table (addrman lite?) would have to be filled with entries, and that source needs to be as similar to everyone else as possible. In Tor, that's the centralized directory to avoid fingerprinting. For this PR, the answer is "DNS seeds". Extending it to "seeds + gossip with seed provenance per job" would also work. If reused across jobs, then the per-tx tracking can continue via similar fingerprinting vectors.

> Would that be a problem with i2p in general, and not private broadcast? I'm not sure I understand how a sybil attack in i2p could leak a clearnet IP address.

> How would sybiling the node affect sending private broadcast transactions through ephemeral i2p tunnels? These connections should not be connected in any way to the broadcasting node's long-lived i2p address (if it has one) or their tor onion address or clearnet addresses.

It's specific to the private broadcast implementation, not the i2p protocol itself. The population of i2p is small, thus making your i2p-supporting victim node more predisposed to connect to an attacker.

Once the attacker is a recipient, it can act on a suspect over clearnet before, during or after its private connection. The crux is whether it still gets an INV from the victim, and whether that INV depends on what it did. In master it can (#36277 fixed one case). In this PR the job announces on a schedule drawn at job start, and nothing the job receives or sees of the transaction changes that, so the attacker gets the same INV whatever it does.

This entire line of attack collapses by construction and we can be a little less "careful" on which endpoint we connect to, falling back to reasoning about liveness rather than privacy.

> Since we no longer make any promises, and this is marked experimental, can we elaborate on the attacks it cannot resist? I find it difficult to reason about the tradeoffs presented here with respect to attacks that I do not understand or know about. Similarly with the above claims about peer influence and i2p sybiling. Wasn't part of the benefit of marking experimental to allow these attacks and weaknesses to be discussed openly?

To answer directly: I don't think experimental makes publishing working attacks ok. I think talking about the serial issues the feature has had publicly patched and extrapolating beyond that is more than sufficient to draw lessons.

The fixes so far: #35032 (addrman updated from private connections), #35410 (v1 retry went over clearnet), #36277 (what recipients saw depended on receipt timing) and #36312 (discouragement of a private peer was observable). Each is a separate place where private broadcast shares state or code with the node, and each was found after merge. Private broadcast connections still run through the node's connection manager, message processing and peer state. The useful question is how we'd know we've found the last one. This PR removes the sharing.

I think marking it as experimental has two considerations:

1. API breaks. They happen even in the case where something is technically perfect. Should have been the case from the get-go.
2. Failure to achieve stated aims. If our stated aims were to mildly frustrate known adversaries like a strawman-passive LinkingLion (connect and stay quiet), I would say it's unnecessary to mark it experimental. (We also had a bug that broke even this, #35410, fixed in v31.1. Assume for the sake of argument there are no others like it.)

The issue is that this is not true. It currently fails to achieve what I believe the stated aim is, at a fundamental level. I think this is close: it should resist an attacker that "runs many bitcoin nodes and then is able to correlate incoming (decrypted) traffic to originating IP address" (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29415#issuecomment-2295439986). That description covers the active version too: an attacker that holds recipient slots and probes suspects over clearnet. That's where master falls short. Finding and building attacks like this is cheap now, so we should defend against the stated model unless that's impossible. The aim of the specification (and thus implementation, if correct) is to directly address this security model.

The spec in this PR states its goals and invariants against that adversary. The tests here check the IP-linkage invariants, with more on the follow-up branch. I think anyone doubting that a fresh attempt at the problem is needed should be looking at what is in master, and figuring out which invariants it holds, and how they are validated.

> > The design doc looks AI written; is it meant for human or agentic consumption?
> 
> The PR text is AI written, curated a number of times under my direction as the primary document. I think there's great value for both humans and AI. It doesn't have to be in the merged branch.

FWIW, it feels overly long, and poorly focused to me; same as most AI spec work. It doesn't really give you a TLDR high-level summary, mixes high level and low level stuff in the same sentence, and makes up its own unnecessary jargon (eg: "Attempt: an opportunity that is dialled: one proxy stream, one BIP324 connection, one session.") Which is fine for an implementation artifact from while you're exploring a feature, and also fine for AI's who like that sort of thing anyway, just seems more negative than positive as a published design doc.

> > Shouldn't it be a BIP, or at least posted to the mailing list for broader discussion on exactly the sort of tradeoffs vasild raises [#36628 (comment)](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36628#issuecomment-6413061893)?
> 
> I think there's definitely value increasing anonymity set if nothing else. By the same token, the current implementation should have gone through a BIP process, for exactly the same reasons.

Better late than never? *shrug*

> > That approach
> 
> Originally I designed it as a separate tool, but I was hoping for a like-for-like replacement.

I mostly think this PR is way too much work for the value it gets. I seem to be thinking that about a lot of things though.

Looking through my node's logs (long lived ipv4 ip and tor address) over the past few months, I saw 0 private broadcast connections in July, 9 in August (4 didn't send an INV at all, 3 accepted, 1 rejected for insufficient fee, 1 already have), 12 in September (3 didn't send an INV, 2 accepted, 1 rejected for fee, 6 already have), 9 in October so far (4 no INV, 1 accepted, 4 already have). Multiply 3 accepted by 18k listening nodes gives 55k txs/month vs ~20M txs in October so far, so perhaps 0.28% of transaction volume. That usage level doesn't feel like it warrants huge PRs to me.

Could also plausibly just add the hook, and let the implementation live entirely out of tree, with any privacy issues dealt with externally. Then re-merge it, and add wallet support, only once the feature has proven itself robust.

> > Since we no longer make any promises, and this is marked experimental, can we elaborate on the attacks it cannot resist? I find it difficult to reason about the tradeoffs presented here with respect to attacks that I do not understand or know about. Similarly with the above claims about peer influence and i2p sybiling. Wasn't part of the benefit of marking experimental to allow these attacks and weaknesses to be discussed openly?
> 
> To answer directly: I don't think experimental makes publishing working attacks ok. I think talking about the serial issues the feature has had publicly patched and extrapolating beyond that is more than sufficient to draw lessons.

I think there's three ways you could consider a feature:

 * purely research -- nobody's implemented or using it, people are exploring the idea to see if it works, no real reason not to discuss attacks openly
 * best effort -- this approach gives an improvement on alternatives (just broadcast on clearnet) in the average case, but doesn't really  provide any guarantees against the worst case
 * fully supported -- this is intended to provide guarantees, many people are relying and would be harmed if attacks become more widely known

Personally, I don't think private broadcast should be considered fully supported, and I think the amount of re-thinking it seems to need along with fairly low adoption suggests it could even be more "purely research" than "best effort". I think not talking about the potential attacks probably makes it harder to move towards fully supported rather than easier, as well.

> The issue is that this is not true. It currently fails to achieve what I believe the stated aim is, at a fundamental level.

I don't think enabling privatebroadcast makes things worse for any of these privacy concerns compared to running the same node in the same adversarial environment with privatebroadcast disabled, and in many cases makes them better. I'd call that meeting the aims ("improves the privacy of the transaction originator"), even if it's far from perfect or was overhyped ("If the originator sends two otherwise unrelated transactions, they will not be linkable").

> That usage level doesn't feel like it warrants huge PRs to me.

That's sort of an argument for ripping it out entirely. Which granted you sort of follow up with immediately afte.

My argument for keeping it, in replaced form: Yes it's a lot of code, relatively speaking, but it's far easier to reason about than what is in master. There's no interference with consensus critical code, was built for testing in mind, and contains future profile breaks to intentional design decisions. That's not even broaching the subject of the IP address leaks.

If that's "too much work", we should remove it entirely, replaced with maybe a hook like you say.

> I don't think enabling privatebroadcast makes things worse for any of these privacy concerns compared to running the same node in the same adversarial environment with privatebroadcast disabled, and in many cases makes them better. I'd call that meeting the aims ("improves the privacy of the transaction originator"), even if it's far from perfect or was overhyped ("If the originator sends two otherwise unrelated transactions, they will not be linkable").

I think there is very little we can say about today's implementation to the user, and incremental whackamole improvements doesn't look like it will change that. "best effort with no described privacy model forever" <-- is this something we should be supporting

events.message:
doc: add the private broadcast specification

This is the design the following commits implement: what a private
broadcast job guarantees, the values peers and observers see, and the
node's interface. Later commits cite its items by number.

privbcast: add the parameters and the schedule

Start src/privbcast, the code that will run the node's private
broadcast jobs, built into bitcoin_node. params.h holds the values of
the specification. DrawPlan draws a job's plan from the job's own
randomness: the schedule, the order of the DNS seeds and the seed of
the order in which each DNS seed hands out its candidates.
MIN_DNS_SEEDS is the floor R3 sets for the mainnet seed list, and a
unit test holds the list to it, so a release that drops seeds below
what fills a job fails the test rather than leaving opportunities
empty.

Implements C1 and R3; the values of Parameters.

privbcast: add candidate assignment

Assign fixes every opportunity's candidate once discovery ends, from
the plan and the discovery result alone. An endpoint that several
seeds returned is credited to the seed that comes first in the plan's
seed order, through the lowest query set that returned it. Each seed
hands out its candidates in an order drawn at random by a generator of
its own, seeded from the plan and the seed's place in that order. Slot
j's first attempt comes from query set j mod 4 whenever a seed it may
draw from has one, so a single exit supplies at most two first
attempts. Neither which seed answers first nor the order of a seed's
answers changes the assignment.

Implements C2, R2, R4, R5a, R5b and R5c.

privbcast: add a byte-driven SOCKS5 client

A job reaches recipients and resolves DNS seed names through the proxy,
on streams its event loop drives without blocking. Socks5Client holds
no socket: it offers the bytes to write, consumes the proxy's replies,
and leaves bytes past the final reply to the P2P transport. It offers
only username and password authentication, with the credentials it is
given or fresh ones, and fails before sending anything if they are
outside RFC 1929's lengths or the username would select Tor's extended
parameters. It sends every destination as a name, numeric addresses
included, and resolves nothing: the node's own connections do the
same, and Tor's SafeSocks refuses a request that carries only an
address. Its errors name the proxy's reply with netbase's
Socks5ErrorString, now exported.

Implements B2 and the Proxy interface section.

privbcast: add the attempt state machine

An attempt is one connection to a recipient once the proxy connected
it: a BIP324 session as initiator, the handshake with the job's
VERSION, one INV, the transaction served at most once, and the PING.
It holds no socket and reads no clock: the job's loop passes the bytes
read and the time; each call records what happened (a completed write,
the connection, bytes received) and then enforces the attempt's
deadlines, so that nothing is acted on at or after one.

The attempt draws its VERSION and PING nonces from the random context
it is given, and takes its BIP324 key, ellswift entropy and garbage
from a key source. Without one, as in production, V2Transport draws
them from the strong RNG. The fuzz target injects a source
that draws from its seeded context, so that an attempt's bytes are a
function of that context and of what the peer sent.

Implements E1-E8, A2, B4, D3 and the attempt part of D2.

privbcast: add proxy streams and discovery

A job reaches the network only through streams to the SOCKS5 proxy,
which its event loop drives without blocking. ProxyStream connects to
the proxy by address or unix socket path, resolving nothing, and runs
the exchange of its Socks5Client; each stage, the connect and each
step of the exchange, times out on the steady clock. Once the proxy
has connected the stream, its socket carries the destination's bytes.

Discovery launches every RESOLVE query at job start, each on a stream
of its own, in four query sets: each set has credentials of its own
and one query of every seed, so Tor builds four circuits rather than
one per query, and each seed is still asked through four exits.
Discovery ends when every query has ended or when the discovery window
does, whatever is still pending. It keeps the answers that are public
routable IPv4 or IPv6 addresses, with the chain's default port, and
counts the others; its result gives each seed's answers by the query
set they came through, whatever order they arrived in. An exception
thrown while it acts on one query ends only that query, as a failed
stream would.

Implements B1, B2, C3, D1, R1, R2 and C7 for the queries.

privbcast: add the job

A job is one event loop on its caller's thread. Step() runs the
deadlines and the dials that are due, waits on every open stream until
the next deadline, and does the I/O; Run() steps to the end. The plan
is drawn when the job is made, before any socket exists, and discovery
starts with the first step. When discovery ends the assignment is
fixed, and each slot dials its opportunities at their scheduled times,
one attempt at a time, until one reaches the announcement point or
none is left; a job whose discovery found no candidate ends there,
failed with "no candidates". The slots share only the loop, so a stalled stream holds
up no other slot, and the cancel flag ends everything at the next step.

An exception thrown while the loop acts on one attempt ends only that
attempt, as a failed stream would. One thrown anywhere else in a step
fails the job: it stops as a cancelled job does, and its report gives
the error.

The report mirrors Interface/Report, every time an offset from job
start on the plan clock. Snapshot() gives the progress the node is to
show, from any thread.

Implements A1, A3, A4, C1-C8, D1, D2, H1-H3 and the report interface.

test: extend the harness for private broadcast jobs

The SOCKS5 server gains Tor's RESOLVE command, reply delays for a slow
or stalled proxy, a mode that offers only unauthenticated access and a
mode that behaves as an ordinary non-Tor proxy. A client that hangs up
before its greeting, as a cancelled job's streams can, and a connection
that Windows reports as aborted count as closed, not as errors. The P2P
network thread judges a failed protocol by its own reconnect flag, so
that several listeners can share one loop. test_framework/privbcast.py
holds the release's parameters, a scripted recipient, and the checks of
a job's wire profile, of fresh keys and nonces in each attempt, and of
its schedule, report summary and proxy credentials.

Prepares the functional tests of the node's jobs.

node: add the private broadcast job queue

The node runs each private broadcast as a privbcast::Job on a thread of
its own. PrivbcastQueue queues the submitted transactions, starts and
cancels the jobs from one scheduler thread, and keeps in memory the
records that getprivatebroadcastinfo and abortprivatebroadcast are to
show. It reaches the node only through callbacks for networking, the
onion proxy and the mempool, and takes the job runner as a parameter,
so that tests can drive it with stub jobs and mocked clocks. A job that
failed, or whose runner threw, ends aborted with the error in its
record. Whether a cancel cut a job short is read from its report, so
one that lands after the job ended leaves it done. At shutdown the
default log gives the number of jobs stopped, and nothing more.

The scheduler's start rule is a pure function, StartPolicy::Decide(),
which each pass of the scheduler applies.

Implements N3-N7, N9, N10, the node's D2 and D3, U3. Not yet wired:
the next commit switches -privatebroadcast to it.

node: run private broadcast as jobs

With -privatebroadcast, sendrawtransaction now queues a job on the
node's PrivbcastQueue instead of handing the transaction to the
connection manager, getprivatebroadcastinfo lists the jobs with their
progress and reports, and abortprivatebroadcast aborts them. Startup
requires onion to be able to become reachable, refuses the regtest
seed and time divisor overrides on other chains, on signet
-signetseednode and -signetchallenge, and off regtest a non-zero
-mocktime, requires -privatebroadcastseed on regtest, which has no DNS
seeds, and refuses to start rather than trim connections when the
jobs' file descriptors are not available. -connect and -proxyrandomize
no longer matter.

-privatebroadcasttimedivisor, regtest only, divides every duration of
a job's plan, so that functional tests can run jobs in real time.

The old private broadcast connections and relay stay in the tree, no
longer fed, until the commits that remove them.

Implements N1, N2, N8, N10, N11, U1, U2 and Interface/Node; replaces
the old implementation's tests with the specification's.

test: run private broadcast jobs end to end through the node

p2p_private_broadcast.py drives jobs on a mocked clock, which moves a
job's schedule but not the steady clock that times its proxy exchanges
and connections. These tests run jobs in real time instead, shortened
by -privatebroadcasttimedivisor: a recipient that floods a job is cut
off at the receive cap, and a proxy that refuses authentication or is
not Tor gets nothing to carry.

test_framework/privbcast.py gains the harness: it restarts the node
behind each scenario's SOCKS5 server with its seeds and time divisor,
and reads the job's report from getprivatebroadcastinfo.

net: remove the old private broadcast relay

Since -privatebroadcast runs jobs, nothing hands PeerManager a
transaction for private broadcast any more. Remove its queue
(src/private_broadcast.{h,cpp}) with the methods, the retry task and
the private_broadcast option that served it, and its handling of
private broadcast connections: the fixed VERSION, the INV after
VERACK, the GETDATA and PONG handling, the incoming message filter,
the lifetime limit and the exemption from discouragement. The unit and
fuzz tests of that code go with it, including the net_tests case for
the addrman exception and the denialofservice_tests cases for the
discouragement exemption.

Delete-only: besides whole lines, conditions and arguments are cut out
of lines, and the lines of a removed branch's alternative move out one
indentation level. git show -w --word-diff-regex='[A-Za-z0-9_]+|[^[:space:]]'
shows deletions only, apart from the size of the node array in
denialofservice_tests, which goes back from 5 to 3.

net: remove the old private broadcast connections

With the relay gone, nothing asks CConnman for private broadcast
connections. Remove the connection type, the thread that opened such
connections with its counters and choice of network, and the places
that treated them specially: the incoming nonce check, the fresh I2P
session, the guard against direct connections, the outbound message
filter, the fixed protocol version, the exception in disconnection by
subnet and their term in the orphanage's static_assert. The type's
names go from getpeerinfo's help, bitcoin-cli -netinfo and the GUI. The
proxy override of ConnectNode() and OpenNetworkConnection(), which only
that thread set, goes too, with its copy in CNode and in the
reconnection record and the fuzz input for it.

Delete-only: besides whole lines, conditions, arguments and list
separators are cut out of lines, what followed a cut argument joins
its line, and one line moves out an indentation level with the if
around it. git show -w --word-diff-regex='[A-Za-z0-9_]+|[^[:space:]]'
shows deletions only.

refactor: drop the trivial AdvertisedVersion()

Without private broadcast connections, a node advertises
PROTOCOL_VERSION on every connection, and CNode::AdvertisedVersion()
only returns it. Use the constant again where the method was called.

doc: describe bitcoind -privatebroadcast

Add the user guide to private broadcast: which Tor proxy the jobs use,
how sendrawtransaction queues them and when they start, what is not
queued again, how to follow and abort jobs, what disabling networking
and shutdown do, which node settings do not apply, what the default
log shows, the file descriptors the jobs need, and the limits of what
a job protects.
doc: release notes for private broadcast jobs

events.body:
> Since we no longer make any promises, and this is marked experimental, can we elaborate on the attacks it cannot resist?

That we mark it experimental in new releases does not automatically notify users that may depend on it because of the misleading claims we made in previous releases.

It's also unnecessary to put these users at risk, as we can discuss the architectural defects without the details of the node state leaks that allow to exploit those.

> find it difficult to reason about the tradeoffs presented here with respect to attacks that I do not understand or know about.

The general pattern is pretty simple. The victim node connects to the attacker both on clearnet and through the private broadcast connection. The attacker correlates the node state on both connections, giving away the privatebroadcasting node's IP address.

Having a non-trivial chance of getting selected for outbound connections costs very little to an attacker. Preventing that a single entity does not occupy all our outbound slots is a design goal of Addrman, but preventing that we don't make a single connection to an attacker with a lot of reachable nodes is not one, nor something we can achieve. Stated differently: it is trivial for today's spies to have the vast majority of Bitcoin nodes connect to them, and then have a non-trivial chance of getting connected to for a private broadcast connection.

_(I'll pass on the terrible incentive for spies to Sybil the network created by the current implementation of this feature.)_

Therefore the only place where we can give meaningful guarantees, is in preventing a private broadcast connection from being correlated with the victim node's connection. This is not something we can guarantee for 2 connections established by the same node, due to the design of our p2p stack, and as i hope the numerous historical correlation vectors and [private broadcast defects](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36628#issuecomment-6449752844) make clear.

I want to emphasize guaranteeing the absence of leaks here. In these discussions i've seen advocates of the current private broadcast architecture challenge critics to lay out the details of specific leaks, so they can be (dismissed or) patched. **This is backwards.** The onus is on advocates of a feature claiming to offer privacy or security, to convince others that it does actually achieve the stated goals under an acceptable threat model. Accepting the feature as secure by default and asking skeptics to keep coming up with end to end exploits to prove otherwise until they get tired of it, is not a serious way to approach development of a privacy feature.

In this instance, this means giving reasonable assurance that state can't be leaked between a regular connection and a private broadcast connection. I'm always happy to consider arguments to the contrary, but as far as i know the only way to get any such assurance currently, is to isolate the private broadcast connections' from the node's state.

> FWIW, it feels overly long, and poorly focused to me; same as most AI spec work.

I think the design document is useful and correct as is, but i agree it's fair to ask the author of a +6000,-3000 PR that directly follows from that document to put in the effort of organically writing such document.

> I mostly think this PR is way too much work for the value it gets.

I think this applies to the private broadcast version currently in master. It provides categorically weaker privacy than existing solutions, and can't provide any guarantee in adversarial conditions (which are the norm: there *are* entities attempting to deanonymize Bitcoin users today).

The stated goals are valuable, and I think would make for a useful feature to have in Core. But the current implementation does not achieve them. So we are stuck in this (now familiar) position of having taken on all the technical debt without achieving anything meaningful. The default position in this situation should be to correct the mistake by reverting the merge, but i like Greg's more positive approach to try and fix it instead.

It's a big PR, but once the specs are pinned down, the implementation is mostly straightforward. It is also not complicated by having to reason about the interaction with existing (and future) P2P machinery, and implements a valuable feature.

> I don't think enabling privatebroadcast makes things worse for any of these privacy concerns compared to running the same node in the same adversarial environment with privatebroadcast disabled

I strongly disagree. @andrewtoth @vasild as far as i understand you share this opinion? I think this view underpins much of our disagreement on how to approach private broadcast, so it's important to get some common ground here to be able to make progress.

The status quo before opting into the private broadcast option was to opt into using one of the available tools making a one shot Tor connection to a public broadcast API to obfuscate source+links, or opt into `-onlynet=tor` to obfuscate the source only.

Today, you can opt into the private broadcast option, which sounds like it may protect your source IP, but actually may not if you also run your node on clearnet. And despite marking it as experimental, some users may consider it relatively more reliable than an external tool maintained by a single person, because it was released by Bitcoin Core :tm:. Others may switch to using it with *some* expectation of privacy ("surely the Core developers wouldn't release a privacy feature which can be defeated *that* easily, they are just being overly conservative in marking it as experimental").

In both cases, this gives users a false sense of security, which i think ranks pretty high in the list of things Bitcoin Core should be very careful not to do.

Now you may argue there exists some users with a desire for privacy that would neither use the one-shot Tor broadcast tools, nor the `onlynet=tor` option, but would use `-privatebroadcast` AND would not change their behaviour due to thinking they are now private (which falls under the footgun discussed just above). And you may say these users were previously susceptible to existing spies on clearnet, so `-privatebroadcast` is an improvement for them.

That may be true before the spies adapt (which is a tautology in itself: users are secure if nobody cares to attack them), but actually makes things even worse once they do. Now the spy can still deanonymize transactions, but they also Sybil the network and we give them for free a "transactions made by users with a particular desire for privacy" filter!

Therefore, i think we should stop describe the current implementation of this feature a "best effort". It’s an innocuous footgun at best, until people start using it and spies adapt, at which point it becomes actively harmful. I understand this would not be true if we fixed all possible leaks, but i think this PR is the only way to get reasonable assurance about this.

> I think the design document is useful and correct as is, but i agree it's fair to ask the author of a +6000,-3000 PR that directly follows from that document to put in the effort of organically writing such document.

Definitely worth putting in a hand-written design doc that's not targeting reimplementation and I had one before (that suffered rot due to churn). But I think the crux of the current arguments currently don't rest on that document,

To be perfectly clear I believe separating the node state as much as possible from private broadcast is the correct goal. However, I shared some concerns about this approach in an earlier draft here https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/pull/7#issuecomment-6201251786, and the same concerns were raised independently by vasild here https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36628#issuecomment-6413061893. I don't think using the built-in DNS seeds to source addresses for private broadcast is the right approach, and I don't think we should drop i2p or direct tor onion connections.

The latter concern doesn't seem to continue to make sense if we successfully execute separating the rest of the state.

Regarding the former concern: as of today that would require us to continue using addrman. Since this is an experimental feature, I don't think we need to rush to a solution. I don't think this needs to be done by v33, and we can brainstorm for other ways to better source addresses. IMO supplying addresses is also a better interface for a tool, since other consumers could source addresses how they wish (say just give the tool mempool.space's node IPs) without dependence on the built-in seeds.

Are these two tradeoffs acceptable, while taking the rest of the patch? I'm not sure. I understand the security team needs to use discretion when discussing possible vulnerabilities, but the status quo here is quite frustrating I'm sure for both sides. How can we know if the issue with only addrman or tor onions or i2p are realistically exploitable?

> Preventing that a single entity does not occupy all our outbound slots is a design goal of Addrman

From the attacks I've seen, the only ones that have not been patched require an attacker to eclipse the node and swallow all addr messages to be effective. If that's the case, this would be very expensive and the user would have bigger problems. Again, is this tradeoff acceptable, or are there now other attacks that have been discovered?

> The onus is on advocates of a feature claiming to offer privacy or security, to convince others that it does actually achieve the stated goals under an acceptable threat model. Accepting the feature as secure by default and asking skeptics to keep coming up with end to end exploits to prove otherwise until they get tired of it, is not a serious way to approach development of a privacy feature.

I don't think this is an acceptable stance if we want to collaborate on improving this feature. AI will continue to insist there are bugs and leaks that are not realistically possible to exploit.

> I think this view underpins much of our disagreement on how to approach private broadcast, so it's important to get some common ground here to be able to make progress.

> The status quo before opting into the private broadcast option was to opt into using one of the available tools making a one shot Tor connection to a public broadcast API to obfuscate source+links, or opt into -onlynet=tor to obfuscate the source only.

> Now you may argue there exists some users with a desire for privacy that would neither use the one-shot Tor broadcast tools

I think the status quo for most users is just using default broadcast, and everyone desires privacy (but they don't know they desire it until someone reveals to them they've violated it). I think making even the current version default behavior if we detect access to a privacy network (and warning if we can't) would be a vast improvement over the status quo. So I think improving the UX of private broadcast (by adding it to wallet, package relay, synchronous, etc.) on the way to making it default behavior is the correct path forward. That way a sybil attacker will spend a lot more resources to find out transactions that are just the default.

Of course we should continue to harden the privacy against these attacks as well, but I don't think the status quo makes this feature less valuable or somehow dangerous to users.

> Looking through my node's logs

Indeed but this is an optional feature that has only been available since last release. I wouldn't expect it to have lots of usage until node-in-a-box implementations start turning it on by default at least.

> The status quo before opting into the private broadcast option was to opt into using one of the available tools making a one shot Tor connection to a public broadcast API to obfuscate source+links, or opt into `-onlynet=tor` to obfuscate the source only.

I think what we have is better than nothing, but I believe the argument you're making is that the relevant alternative isn't nothing, but rather people using an independent tool like https://github.com/alfred-hodler/pushtx and that doing so is better than what we have now (because, being independent, it doesn't risk leaks due to node state contamination).

A quick AI analysis suggests that pushtx has its own failings: if tor isn't available it will just drop to clearnet, it gets the peers to connect to via clearnet DNS, and it allows its connections to be correlated to each other by listening for and reacting to the INV for its own transaction. The alternative approach of using tor to connect to a block explorer's push-tx api endpoint works for privacy, but is obviously pretty terrible for censorship resistance. So I think I'm not really convinced that what we have, even with its flaws, isn't better than the actual alternatives. (I think I am convinced that improving those alternatives is a better path than trying to have an in-node solution that's not contaminated by in-node state though)

> Today, you can opt into the private broadcast option, which sounds like it may protect your source IP, but actually may not if you also run your node on clearnet. And despite marking it as experimental, some users may consider it relatively more reliable than an external tool maintained by a single person, because it was released by Bitcoin Core ™️. Others may switch to using it with _some_ expectation of privacy ("surely the Core developers wouldn't release a privacy feature which can be defeated _that_ easily, they are just being overly conservative in marking it as experimental").

I think it's a mistake in both theory and practice for people to assume Core developers are infallible with regard to crypto or privacy concerns. Getting things right is a matter of correcting mistakes when they occur, not never making mistakes. Trying to satisfy people who expect us never to make mistakes isn't going to work -- the best we can possibly do is satisfy people who expect that we'll tell them when we make mistakes and that we'll do our best to fix those mistakes.

I think you might want to review #35858 as the recommendations there seem stronger than is justified ("The transaction reaches the wider network only once a recipient relays it, which prevents linking the submission to the node's IP address.")

In any event, it sounds to me like a better approach to this feature would be:

 * abandon the approach of in-node support for private broadcast -- there's too much risk of state contamination that defeats the entire purpose of the feature for realistic adversarial scenarios
 * deprecate the existing feature in point updates to existing releases -- what we have isn't something we can really recommend that people use (change it to `-privatebroadcast=allow-deprecated` to continue enabling it perhaps)
 * provide a BIP/spec for private broadcast behaviour, with discussion of the tradeoffs and risks. if different people strongly prefer different approaches, have multiple BIPs as appropriate
 * provide external tools implementing the approach documented in the spec(s)
 * add a hook so that `sendrawtransaction` always uses a specified external tool
 * add a hook so that wallet broadcast (and wallet rebroadcast) always uses a specified external tool rather than adding to the mempool or relaying directly (goal here would be to reduce linkage between txs in different wallets, I think)
 * include an in-repo implementation of a spec whose tradeoffs are reasonable/broadly acceptable and bundle it with bitcoind

I don't have a strong preference as to order; but deprecating the feature shouldn't be delayed pending other steps if our feature either is not something we can recommend as fit for purpose and/or is worse than using alternative third party tools.

(Even in this scenario, there's a potential linkage between node and tx: the wallet will likely only rebroadcast once the tx in question exits your mempool)

Apart from "include an in-repo implementation of a spec" I think all of those should be relatively small or negative-LOC PRs as far as the bitcoin core repo is concerned, so relatively easy to review.

(To clarify maybe: this is my opinion on an approach would most easily meet everyone's goals here; it's not meant to be an ultimatum, or a "your ideas are bad and should be thrown away" against anyone)

> > Preventing that a single entity does not occupy all our outbound slots is a design goal of Addrman
> 
> From the attacks I've seen, the only ones that have not been patched require an attacker to eclipse the node and swallow all addr messages to be effective.

I think an extreme attack scenario worth thinking about here is:

 * about 50% of the reachable addresses in your addrman that also function as a working node (ie, will give you a good headers chain, respond to pings etc) are honest nodes. this is sufficient for addrman's goal of "preventing a single entity from occupying all outbound slots" with 99% chance
 * the remaining 50% of reachable addresses in your addrman (or more, given the additional constraints above) are attacker controlled
 * not only that, most of them (say 42% of addrman entries) are roughly unique to your node -- they were given to only you by the attacker, and you didn't successfully relay them to an honest outbound, because addr relay is probabilistic not flood fill).
 * when you make three outbound connections to do private broadcast, you have ~80% chance of one of those connections being to an attacker controlled address that has not been shared with anyone else, linking that transaction with your node (because the attacker only gave that address to your node), and hence with your other transactions

Hopefully that exact attack is unrealistic, given the expectation that the attacker has to provide perhaps ~650M unique addresses in total (18k addresses for each of 18k public nodes to be 50% of reachable addresses, but unique for each node?) all with a reachable bitcoin node answering them, ready to spy on relayed transactions. It's meant to be a thought-experiment, not an attack recipe, after all.

In that scenario, addrman, block relay and transaction relay all continue to work as specced and the node is not eclipsed, because you do have at least one honest outbound connection, but a pervasive group attempting to do tx linking still immediately succeeds in identifying 4-out-of-5 private broadcast txs.

> Since this is an experimental feature, I don't think we need to rush to a solution.

> I think making even the current version default behavior

> Indeed but this is an optional feature that has only been available since last release. I wouldn't expect it to have lots of usage until node-in-a-box implementations start turning it on by default at least.

I don't think you can reasonably say "this is an experimental feature" and "it should be default and enabled by node-in-a-box implementations" at the same time.

@@ -0,0 +1,478 @@
+# Private broadcast: specification
+
+`bitcoind -privatebroadcast` broadcasts a transaction without revealing the sender. This document states what a job must guarantee (invariants), the values peers and observers
+see (parameters), what the design relies on (assumptions) and what it does not attempt (non-goals).
+How to use it is in [private-broadcast.md](../private-broadcast.md).
+A job carries one transaction. The rationale at the end is not normative.
+
+## Goals
+
+- **GOAL-1.** A job does not reveal the sender's IP address, onion address or long-term node
+  identity to any party.
+- **GOAL-2.** A hostile recipient, DNS seed or Tor exit learns no more about the sender than an
+  honest one. It can only affect delivery.
+
+The invariants are the testable form of these goals.
+
+## Terms
+
+- **Job**: one broadcast of one transaction, from submission to report.
+- **Slot**: one of a job's six delivery targets, each with its own times and candidates.
+- **Opportunity**: one of a slot's four scheduled connection times, a first attempt and up to three
+  backups, each with a pre-assigned candidate or none.
+- **Attempt**: an opportunity that is dialled: one proxy stream, one BIP324 connection, one session.
+- **Announcement point**: the moment the transport accepts the job's INV for sending.
+- **Candidate**: an IPv4 or IPv6 address from a DNS seed, reached through a Tor exit (an exit
+  path).
+- **Query set**: one of a job's QUERIES_PER_SEED sets of discovery credentials, numbered from 0,
+  carrying one RESOLVE query of every DNS seed. Tor gives each set its own circuit.
+- **Delivery start**: job start plus the discovery window.
+
+## Threat model
+
+- A **recipient** sees a Tor exit, the constant profile (E1) and the transaction it is sent.
+- A **Tor exit** sees the recipient's address. BIP324 authenticates nobody, so the exit can also
+  act as the peer: see the transaction, and drop or alter that one connection. The exit of a query
+  set sees that set's query of every seed, and can answer all of them falsely.
+- A **DNS seed**, or the resolver an exit uses, sees queries for the seed names from Tor exits. It
+  can answer falsely. It learns that a job ran.
+- A **network observer** sees the transaction appear at several peers within seconds. That reveals
+  that private broadcast was used, not where the sender is.
+- An **observer between the sender and its Tor guard** (the ISP, or the guard) sees a burst of new
+  circuits when a job starts and single circuits at its scheduled times, not their destinations.
+- The **node's own peers** (node mode) see the transaction only after it has come back from the
+  network, relayed like any other.
+
+## Invariants
+
+Times in the invariants hold to the precision of a step. A job, and the node's queue, act in steps:
+each step reads the clocks and does what is due. Something due at a time happens at or after that
+time, no later than the first step that begins at or after it. A deadline takes effect at or after
+it, and no later than the first step that begins after it, so a step that begins at the deadline
+may still act. Dials go by the clocks as read once the step's I/O is done: however long the I/O
+takes, an opportunity those clocks put more than START_GRACE late is missed, not dialled (C5).
+
+### A. Separation from the node and from other jobs
+
+- **A1.** A job's only inputs are the transaction, the proxy endpoint, the chain's release seed
+  material (DNS seed names, default port), a cancel signal, the clock and fresh randomness.
+- **A2.** Every byte a job sends on a connection is a function of the transaction, per-attempt
+  randomness (BIP324 keys and garbage, VERSION and PING nonces), the messages that peer sent on that
+  connection and when they arrived against the attempt's fixed deadlines, and cancellation. So a
+  peer that declines, never asks or never answers the PING sees the same bytes as a cooperative one
+  up to that point; only when the connection closes differs.
+- **A3.** No state written by the node or by another job changes what a job sends or when. A job
+  keeps no state of its own on disk and leaves the node's peers, address manager and ban list as
+  they were.
+- **A4.** Apart from the transaction and the release profile, nothing a job sends or presents is
+  shared between two attempts or two jobs: BIP324 keys and garbage, VERSION and PING nonces and
+  proxy credentials are fresh per attempt or query set, and the schedule is fresh per job.
+
+### B. Network path
+
+- **B1.** Every stream a job opens goes through the SOCKS5 proxy. There is no direct connection and
+  no local DNS lookup.
+- **B2.** Each attempt's stream carries fresh random isolation credentials, and so does each query
+  set: its RESOLVE streams share them, and nothing else does. This holds whatever the node's proxy
+  settings. A proxy that does not accept username and password authentication gets no stream.
+- **B3.** A job uses the node's configured onion proxy, local or not, trusted like its other proxy
+  settings; the path to a remote proxy sees every destination and can tell job streams from the
+  node's by their credentials.
+- **B4.** Every attempt is BIP324 v2 as initiator. There is no v1 fallback.
+
+### C. Fixed plan
+
+- **C1.** The schedule, every opportunity's start and deadline, is drawn at job start, before any
+  network activity, independently of anything the job observes.
+- **C2.** Every opportunity's candidate is fixed when discovery ends, before any recipient is
+  contacted, as a function of the discovery result alone.
+- **C3.** Discovery ends when every query has completed or when the discovery window ends, whichever
+  comes first. Delivery starts at job start plus the discovery window, whatever discovery did.
+  Answers arriving after the window are discarded.
+- **C4.** Nothing received on a connection and nothing seen of the transaction's propagation
+  changes any time, any assignment or which opportunities run. The only exceptions: a slot's
+  failure before the announcement point lets its next pre-assigned opportunity run at its scheduled
+  time, and an announcement stops the slot's remaining opportunities. So a recipient can affect
+  only its own slot, whether the slot's remaining opportunities run and when it ends, and through
+  that when the job ends. There are no retries beyond the pre-drawn opportunities.
+- **C5.** An opportunity that has a candidate is dialled at most START_GRACE after its scheduled
+  time, unless its slot has already announced (C6) or the job has been cancelled (C8). An
+  opportunity the job cannot dial by then is missed, never dialled late.
+- **C6.** Before the announcement point an attempt is replaceable; after it nothing else in that
+  slot runs. Reports count an announcement only once the INV is fully written; the difference is
+  presentation only.
+- **C7.** Slots run independently. No slot waits for, or is limited by, another slot. An internal
+  failure in one attempt or one discovery query ends only that attempt or query, as a transport
+  error would. A failure before the attempt exists leaves its opportunity missed (C5).
+- **C8.** Cancellation stops the whole job in the step that sees it, without waiting for any
+  deadline: blocked proxy exchanges and connects to the proxy under way are abandoned, and no
+  opportunity starts after that step.
+
+### D. Bounds
+
+- **D1.** A job makes at most SLOTS × OPPORTUNITIES_PER_SLOT recipient connections, at most SLOTS
+  at once. Its discovery has QUERIES_PER_SEED query sets, so as many circuits, each with at most
+  one RESOLVE stream per DNS seed, all launched at job start.
+- **D2.** An attempt ends by its scheduled start plus ATTEMPT_MAX. A slot ends when its announced
+  attempt ends, or when every one of its opportunities has ended: an attempt when it ends, an
+  opportunity without a candidate at its scheduled time, a missed one when it is missed (C5). So it
+  ends by its last opportunity's scheduled start plus ATTEMPT_MAX, its scheduled end, which is at
+  most SLOT_MAX after its first opportunity. The job ends when its last slot has ended, at most
+  SCHEDULED_BOUND after job start, or, if discovery found no candidate, when discovery ends: it has
+  nothing to dial, and fails with "no candidates" (H2). Nothing is acted on once a phase deadline
+  has passed. These bounds are on the wall clock, so a clock set back mid-run stretches what
+  remains, and one set forward past an opportunity by more than START_GRACE makes it missed (C5):
+  the job can then end `done` without a connection, or fail with "no candidates" if its discovery
+  is overtaken. The node stops a job still running JOB_CAP after it started, measured on a steady
+  clock.
+- **D3.** A connection that has received more than MAX_RECV_BYTES, counting every byte read from it
+  after the proxy connected it, is ended. This is a sanity bound, not part of the privacy model.
+  The node queues at most MAX_QUEUED_JOBS jobs and refuses further submissions; the bound is on the
+  number of jobs, not their size. It keeps at most MAX_FINISHED_JOBS reports.
+
+### E. Wire behaviour on every connection
+
+- **E1.** The job's VERSION is identical for every job of a release except its nonce (see
+  Parameters).
+- **E2.** The job announces only after the peer's VERSION shows a version of at least
+  MIN_PEER_PROTOCOL_VERSION, NODE_WITNESS and relay, and the peer has sent WTXIDRELAY before its
+  VERACK. After such a VERSION the job sends WTXIDRELAY, then VERACK; after any other it sends
+  nothing more. A VERSION that lacks a field up to the relay flag, has bytes after it, or whose
+  user agent is longer than 256 bytes, is another. A peer that fails any of
+  these is left before the announcement.
+- **E3.** The job sends exactly one INV, with one entry: MSG_WTX for the announced transaction's
+  wtxid.

@@ -0,0 +1,478 @@
+# Private broadcast: specification
+
+`bitcoind -privatebroadcast` broadcasts a transaction without revealing the sender. This document states what a job must guarantee (invariants), the values peers and observers
+see (parameters), what the design relies on (assumptions) and what it does not attempt (non-goals).
+How to use it is in [private-broadcast.md](../private-broadcast.md).
+A job carries one transaction. The rationale at the end is not normative.
+
+## Goals
+
+- **GOAL-1.** A job does not reveal the sender's IP address, onion address or long-term node
+  identity to any party.
+- **GOAL-2.** A hostile recipient, DNS seed or Tor exit learns no more about the sender than an
+  honest one. It can only affect delivery.
+
+The invariants are the testable form of these goals.
+
+## Terms
+
+- **Job**: one broadcast of one transaction, from submission to report.
+- **Slot**: one of a job's six delivery targets, each with its own times and candidates.
+- **Opportunity**: one of a slot's four scheduled connection times, a first attempt and up to three
+  backups, each with a pre-assigned candidate or none.
+- **Attempt**: an opportunity that is dialled: one proxy stream, one BIP324 connection, one session.
+- **Announcement point**: the moment the transport accepts the job's INV for sending.
+- **Candidate**: an IPv4 or IPv6 address from a DNS seed, reached through a Tor exit (an exit
+  path).
+- **Query set**: one of a job's QUERIES_PER_SEED sets of discovery credentials, numbered from 0,
+  carrying one RESOLVE query of every DNS seed. Tor gives each set its own circuit.
+- **Delivery start**: job start plus the discovery window.
+
+## Threat model
+
+- A **recipient** sees a Tor exit, the constant profile (E1) and the transaction it is sent.
+- A **Tor exit** sees the recipient's address. BIP324 authenticates nobody, so the exit can also
+  act as the peer: see the transaction, and drop or alter that one connection. The exit of a query
+  set sees that set's query of every seed, and can answer all of them falsely.
+- A **DNS seed**, or the resolver an exit uses, sees queries for the seed names from Tor exits. It
+  can answer falsely. It learns that a job ran.
+- A **network observer** sees the transaction appear at several peers within seconds. That reveals
+  that private broadcast was used, not where the sender is.
+- An **observer between the sender and its Tor guard** (the ISP, or the guard) sees a burst of new
+  circuits when a job starts and single circuits at its scheduled times, not their destinations.
+- The **node's own peers** (node mode) see the transaction only after it has come back from the
+  network, relayed like any other.
+
+## Invariants
+
+Times in the invariants hold to the precision of a step. A job, and the node's queue, act in steps:
+each step reads the clocks and does what is due. Something due at a time happens at or after that
+time, no later than the first step that begins at or after it. A deadline takes effect at or after
+it, and no later than the first step that begins after it, so a step that begins at the deadline
+may still act. Dials go by the clocks as read once the step's I/O is done: however long the I/O
+takes, an opportunity those clocks put more than START_GRACE late is missed, not dialled (C5).
+
+### A. Separation from the node and from other jobs
+
+- **A1.** A job's only inputs are the transaction, the proxy endpoint, the chain's release seed
+  material (DNS seed names, default port), a cancel signal, the clock and fresh randomness.
+- **A2.** Every byte a job sends on a connection is a function of the transaction, per-attempt
+  randomness (BIP324 keys and garbage, VERSION and PING nonces), the messages that peer sent on that
+  connection and when they arrived against the attempt's fixed deadlines, and cancellation. So a
+  peer that declines, never asks or never answers the PING sees the same bytes as a cooperative one
+  up to that point; only when the connection closes differs.
+- **A3.** No state written by the node or by another job changes what a job sends or when. A job
+  keeps no state of its own on disk and leaves the node's peers, address manager and ban list as
+  they were.
+- **A4.** Apart from the transaction and the release profile, nothing a job sends or presents is
+  shared between two attempts or two jobs: BIP324 keys and garbage, VERSION and PING nonces and
+  proxy credentials are fresh per attempt or query set, and the schedule is fresh per job.
+
+### B. Network path
+
+- **B1.** Every stream a job opens goes through the SOCKS5 proxy. There is no direct connection and
+  no local DNS lookup.
+- **B2.** Each attempt's stream carries fresh random isolation credentials, and so does each query
+  set: its RESOLVE streams share them, and nothing else does. This holds whatever the node's proxy
+  settings. A proxy that does not accept username and password authentication gets no stream.
+- **B3.** A job uses the node's configured onion proxy, local or not, trusted like its other proxy
+  settings; the path to a remote proxy sees every destination and can tell job streams from the
+  node's by their credentials.
+- **B4.** Every attempt is BIP324 v2 as initiator. There is no v1 fallback.
+
+### C. Fixed plan
+
+- **C1.** The schedule, every opportunity's start and deadline, is drawn at job start, before any
+  network activity, independently of anything the job observes.
+- **C2.** Every opportunity's candidate is fixed when discovery ends, before any recipient is
+  contacted, as a function of the discovery result alone.
+- **C3.** Discovery ends when every query has completed or when the discovery window ends, whichever
+  comes first. Delivery starts at job start plus the discovery window, whatever discovery did.
+  Answers arriving after the window are discarded.
+- **C4.** Nothing received on a connection and nothing seen of the transaction's propagation
+  changes any time, any assignment or which opportunities run. The only exceptions: a slot's
+  failure before the announcement point lets its next pre-assigned opportunity run at its scheduled
+  time, and an announcement stops the slot's remaining opportunities. So a recipient can affect
+  only its own slot, whether the slot's remaining opportunities run and when it ends, and through
+  that when the job ends. There are no retries beyond the pre-drawn opportunities.
+- **C5.** An opportunity that has a candidate is dialled at most START_GRACE after its scheduled
+  time, unless its slot has already announced (C6) or the job has been cancelled (C8). An
+  opportunity the job cannot dial by then is missed, never dialled late.
+- **C6.** Before the announcement point an attempt is replaceable; after it nothing else in that
+  slot runs. Reports count an announcement only once the INV is fully written; the difference is
+  presentation only.
+- **C7.** Slots run independently. No slot waits for, or is limited by, another slot. An internal
+  failure in one attempt or one discovery query ends only that attempt or query, as a transport
+  error would. A failure before the attempt exists leaves its opportunity missed (C5).
+- **C8.** Cancellation stops the whole job in the step that sees it, without waiting for any
+  deadline: blocked proxy exchanges and connects to the proxy under way are abandoned, and no
+  opportunity starts after that step.
+
+### D. Bounds
+
+- **D1.** A job makes at most SLOTS × OPPORTUNITIES_PER_SLOT recipient connections, at most SLOTS
+  at once. Its discovery has QUERIES_PER_SEED query sets, so as many circuits, each with at most
+  one RESOLVE stream per DNS seed, all launched at job start.
+- **D2.** An attempt ends by its scheduled start plus ATTEMPT_MAX. A slot ends when its announced
+  attempt ends, or when every one of its opportunities has ended: an attempt when it ends, an
+  opportunity without a candidate at its scheduled time, a missed one when it is missed (C5). So it
+  ends by its last opportunity's scheduled start plus ATTEMPT_MAX, its scheduled end, which is at
+  most SLOT_MAX after its first opportunity. The job ends when its last slot has ended, at most
+  SCHEDULED_BOUND after job start, or, if discovery found no candidate, when discovery ends: it has
+  nothing to dial, and fails with "no candidates" (H2). Nothing is acted on once a phase deadline
+  has passed. These bounds are on the wall clock, so a clock set back mid-run stretches what
+  remains, and one set forward past an opportunity by more than START_GRACE makes it missed (C5):
+  the job can then end `done` without a connection, or fail with "no candidates" if its discovery
+  is overtaken. The node stops a job still running JOB_CAP after it started, measured on a steady
+  clock.
+- **D3.** A connection that has received more than MAX_RECV_BYTES, counting every byte read from it
+  after the proxy connected it, is ended. This is a sanity bound, not part of the privacy model.
+  The node queues at most MAX_QUEUED_JOBS jobs and refuses further submissions; the bound is on the
+  number of jobs, not their size. It keeps at most MAX_FINISHED_JOBS reports.
+
+### E. Wire behaviour on every connection
+
+- **E1.** The job's VERSION is identical for every job of a release except its nonce (see
+  Parameters).
+- **E2.** The job announces only after the peer's VERSION shows a version of at least
+  MIN_PEER_PROTOCOL_VERSION, NODE_WITNESS and relay, and the peer has sent WTXIDRELAY before its
+  VERACK. After such a VERSION the job sends WTXIDRELAY, then VERACK; after any other it sends
+  nothing more. A VERSION that lacks a field up to the relay flag, has bytes after it, or whose
+  user agent is longer than 256 bytes, is another. A peer that fails any of
+  these is left before the announcement.
+- **E3.** The job sends exactly one INV, with one entry: MSG_WTX for the announced transaction's
+  wtxid.
comments.body:
1. There's massive profile breaks everywhere in this PR. If we're going to break it, now is the time, especially if usage is low.
2. Aside from simply being widely supported, WTXID relay allows for slightly more robust opportunistic package relay, since moredern Core nodes will only count wtxid relay peers as additional announcers of orphans. There avoids a potential future profile break (or logic that switches flags depending on what is being sent).

### Breakdown of the Code and Discussion
 1. **The Code Change (src/privbcast/params.h)**:
   * **inline constexpr int PROFILE_VERSION{70017};**: Defines the current profile version as 70017.
   * **static_assert(PROFILE_VERSION == PROTOCOL_VERSION, ...);**: A compile-time assertion checking that the profile version matches the core protocol version, with the comment explaining: *"the profile's version tracks the release"*.
 2. **The Feedback (ajtowns - Anthony Towns)**:
   * Points out that 70016 is what current private broadcast versions track. He notes that *avoiding* varying these things across standard releases is precisely why a special profile exists, meaning the profile version shouldn't necessarily be tied directly to changing protocol or release versions haphazardly.
 

   * Agrees that the comment/assertion logic is flawed ("yeah this is a bad comment and probably not needed").
   * Clarifies that changes to this should *not* act as a profile break (which is what the static_assert enforces), and notes that he will change it.
